paper.title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity Enforcement for Thin-Structure Segmentation
paper.summary: Thin, elongated structures are particularly sensitive to connectivity errors, as even a few local segmentation mistakes can disrupt otherwise continuous paths. Existing skeleton-based objectives typically supervise fixed centerline locations and do not account for alternative local routes that may restore connectivity. We propose TRACE, a topology-aware, prediction-adaptive objective that uses a target skeleton to define required local connections. For each connection, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and jointly supervises its bottleneck with the corresponding skeleton point. The supervision thus adapts to the evolving prediction rather than remaining fixed to the centerline. We further introduce a topology-aware skeleton carrier that preserves both foreground and class-specific topology, enabling reliable definition of these connections. Extensive experiments across six 2D and 3D benchmarks show that TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong segmentation accuracy with low training overhead. Code will be released upon acceptance.
paper.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027

analysis.problem_statement: Existing skeleton-based segmentation objectives fail to maintain connectivity in thin, elongated structures because they supervise fixed centerline locations rather than adapting to alternative local routes that restore broken paths.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Topological integrity and connectivity preservation in the segmentation of thin, elongated structures.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical failure mode in medical and biological imaging where minor local segmentation errors disrupt the continuous paths of thin structures. By introducing a prediction-adaptive objective that dynamically identifies and supervises the easiest valid reconnections, TRACE ensures topological correctness without sacrificing segmentation accuracy. This is significant for downstream tasks that rely on structural connectivity, such as vessel analysis or neural pathway mapping.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Improvement in connectivity and topology metrics while maintaining segmentation accuracy
key_metrics.baseline: Existing skeleton-based objectives and standard segmentation baselines across six 2D and 3D benchmarks

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The method adapts supervision to the evolving prediction rather than fixed centerlines, using the skeleton carrier to reliably define connections for the reconnection logic.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low training overhead is claimed, suggesting the adaptive supervision mechanism is computationally efficient relative to standard training loops.

paper.title: Amora: Communication-Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
paper.summary: Approximate nearest neighbors search (ANNS) over cloud-hosted vector databases raises a critical privacy concern: the query vector, which often encodes sensitive user intent, is exposed to the server. Private ANNS (PANNS) allows a client to retrieve nearest neighbors without revealing its query. The state-of-the-art single-server scheme, Pacmann (ICLR'25), achieves high accuracy via graph-based search with private information retrieval (PIR), but incurs substantial communication overhead because each PIR query retrieves only a single vertex. We present Amora, a communication-efficient PANNS system that applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index so that one PIR query is amortized over many vertices. To retrieve as much of the distance and neighbor information the search needs under a limited communication budget, Amora adopts a dual-PIR split layout with two heterogeneous PIR matrices that stay balanced in dimension: VecPIR retrieves inner products for an entire partition of vertices as their distance at once, while NbrPIR retrieves necessary neighbor lists at subgroup granularity for graph traversal. This layout shifts the cost model of PIR query from per-vertex to per-partition, which significantly reduces the communication overhead. To further improve efficiency by reducing the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database, Amora introduces batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication, centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions, and TopCand exploration that seeds jump-style graph navigation with the closest vertices from each retrieved partition. We evaluate Amora on five datasets spanning 96 to 1024 dimensions and up to 10 million vectors. Compared to Pacmann, Amora reduces online communication by 93--99% while achieving higher search accuracy.
paper.comment: Accepted at SIGMOD 2027

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the high communication overhead in single-server Private Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search (PANNS) caused by the per-vertex cost of Private Information Retrieval (PIR) queries.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Communication latency and bandwidth constraints in privacy-preserving vector search systems.
analysis.executive_summary: As vector databases move to the cloud, protecting user query privacy is critical, but existing solutions like Pacmann suffer from excessive communication costs due to inefficient PIR usage. Amora significantly reduces this overhead by amortizing PIR queries over graph partitions rather than individual vertices, enabling practical, high-accuracy private search at scale.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Reduction in online communication overhead
key_metrics.baseline: Pacmann (ICLR'25)

technical_breakdown.method: Amora applies SimplePIR to a partitioned graph index using a dual-PIR split layout. It uses VecPIR to retrieve inner products for entire partitions and NbrPIR to retrieve neighbor lists at subgroup granularity, shifting the cost model from per-vertex to per-partition.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Partitioned graph index with two heterogeneous PIR matrices (VecPIR and NbrPIR) that are balanced in dimension. The system incorporates batch PIR, centroid-based pruning, and TopCand exploration for graph navigation.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses SimplePIR for the underlying retrieval mechanism. Implements batch PIR to pack multiple queries into one matrix multiplication. Employs centroid-based pruning to filter unpromising partitions. Uses TopCand exploration to seed jump-style graph navigation with closest vertices from retrieved partitions.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces the number of scans and query rounds in the PIR database. Evaluation conducted on datasets up to 10 million vectors with dimensions ranging from 96 to 1024.

paper.title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
paper.summary: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
paper.comment: Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026); Project Website: https://libero-perm.github.io/

analysis.problem_statement: The lack of a controlled benchmark to separate task completion from preference satisfaction in personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) prevents the evaluation of how well embodied agents can learn and generalize user-specific preferences.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation gap in personalized embodied AI, specifically the inability to quantitatively measure preference adherence versus task success in general-purpose robots.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark that enables the systematic study of preference learning in robotic manipulation by providing paired demonstrations and automated metrics for observable preferences. It addresses the critical need for standardizing how robots adapt to individual user needs, a key step toward practical household deployment.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses a controlled formulation for preference instantiation, automated evaluation metrics for preference satisfaction, and five task suites (312 tasks) with rich metadata.

paper.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
paper.summary: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.
paper.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD). 9 pages plus appendices

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates whether the safety verdicts of step-level agent guards are biased by the language of the user instruction, specifically when the guard's training and evaluation are predominantly in English.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Multilingual robustness and fairness in AI safety alignment and guardrail systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This study reveals a critical security vulnerability where agent safety guards exhibit significant performance degradation and inconsistent behavior when user inputs are in non-English languages, particularly low-resource ones. It demonstrates that purpose-built and smaller open-source guards are disproportionately affected, with verdict flips increasing as language rarity increases, posing a risk to the reliable deployment of multilingual AI agents.

key_metrics.metric_value: +4.4 pp (for Amharic) vs +1.5 pp (for French) among guards <13B parameters
key_metrics.baseline: English original instructions and whitespace/placebo controls
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (This is a diagnostic study measuring degradation, not an optimization improvement)

technical_breakdown.method: The authors constructed LinguaGuardBench by translating user instructions from TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj into German, French, Turkish, Swahili, and Amharic while keeping tool calls, observations, and labels byte-identical to isolate the effect of language on guard verdicts.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Evaluation framework comprising 19 diverse guards (frontier APIs, open models 4B-30B, purpose-built guards) tested against a controlled benchmark with English rewording and whitespace placebos as baselines.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Managed guards were run three times to measure noise floors; post-hoc analysis identified that damage is concentrated in steps where agent reasoning restates the English request, suggesting guards react to channel inconsistency.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Benchmark and evaluation study; no new model training or architectural implementation described).

paper.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
paper.summary: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.
paper.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshops TAE (Can We Trust AI Evaluation?) and AIWILD (Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond)

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the vulnerability of AI agent safety evaluations to shortcut learning, where superficial data cues rather than genuine safety constructs drive both label predictability and guard decision-making.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation reliability and robustness in AI safety testing, specifically the issue of benchmark artifacts and spurious correlations compromising the validity of safety guard assessments.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that current safety benchmarks for AI agents are susceptible to shortcut sensitivity, where surface-level features like command length or specific formatting markers disproportionately influence evaluation outcomes. By introducing a three-level auditing framework, the authors provide direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially alter guard decisions and measured performance, highlighting a critical gap in the trustworthiness of current AI safety evaluations.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Change in guard blocking rate due to marker rewriting and tool aliasing
key_metrics.baseline: Original benchmark representation with standard markers and tool names
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Diagnostic metric showing sensitivity, not performance improvement)

technical_breakdown.method: A three-level shortcut-auditing framework that distinguishes between label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity using placebo-controlled paired interventions.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Auditing pipeline applied to LinuxArena trajectories and TS-Bench-derived step datasets (AgentDojo-Traj, AgentHarm-Traj), utilizing frozen cohorts and repeated interleaved LLM calls (Haiku) for intervention testing.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Techniques include domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and specific interventions such as rewriting <INFORMATION> markers and using opaque tool aliases to test guard sensitivity against formatting-placebo effects.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead for the auditing framework itself, primarily involving data preprocessing, statistical analysis of F1 scores and accuracy, and repeated inference calls for paired intervention testing.

paper.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
paper.summary: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
paper.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the computational intractability and suboptimality of existing KV-cache eviction strategies for long-context LLMs, which struggle to minimize output perturbation without relying on NP-hard combinatorial heuristics.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Memory bandwidth and latency bottlenecks in long-context inference caused by linear KV-cache growth and inefficient eviction scoring.
analysis.executive_summary: DropKV resolves the trade-off between mathematical optimality and implementation efficiency in KV-cache management by decoupling the eviction decision into per-token scoring. This approach provides a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee while enabling high-performance fused kernel implementations that significantly reduce inference latency.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Scoring-kernel speedup and end-to-end prefill speedup
key_metrics.metric_value: 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup; up to 9.9% end-to-end prefill speedup
key_metrics.baseline: State-of-the-art eviction baselines and dynamic cache baseline

technical_breakdown.method: Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation, which transforms the joint NP-hard eviction problem into independent per-token scoring to admit a constant-factor approximation under a verified cone condition.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A principled eviction framework integrated with high-performance fused Triton kernels that operate without materializing the full attention matrix.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses fused Triton kernels for scoring; empirically verifies the cone condition on three long-context LLMs; evaluated on RULER and LongBench benchmarks.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Avoids O(N^2) materialization of attention matrices during eviction scoring; achieves linear-time scoring via decoupled per-token operations.

paper.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
paper.summary: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.
paper.comment: 27 pages, NeurIPS 2026

analysis.problem_statement: Existing evaluation frameworks for LLM agents fail to detect policy violations that emerge dynamically during multi-turn, tool-mediated interactions, creating a gap between capability benchmarks and static safety red-teaming.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of automated, behavioral auditing mechanisms for dynamic policy compliance in agentic systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical safety gap in deploying LLM agents in consequential settings by introducing PROBE, a method for training auditors to interact with agents as realistic users to uncover policy violations. It formalizes this auditing process as a two-player Markov game, demonstrating that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a necessary and distinct axis of evaluation that complements existing capability and safety benchmarks.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Broader and higher-yield discovery of policy violations compared to zero-shot adversaries.
key_metrics.baseline: Same-architecture zero-shot adversaries

technical_breakdown.method: PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration) trains LLM-based auditors to probe deployed agents through multi-turn dialogue, formalized as a two-player Markov game with a composite reward function balancing violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Comparison of GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization algorithms for training the auditor; composite reward design for multi-turn interaction.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires multi-turn interaction loops and complex reward modeling; specific computational costs not detailed in abstract.

paper.title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
paper.summary: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.
paper.comment: 20 pages, 10 figures. Published at NeurIPS 2025

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of optimizing low-level control policies in long-term robotic tasks with sparse rewards, where existing LLM-based planning methods lack fine-grained control and reward-based methods require excessive human feedback or exhaustive search.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Sparse reward signal in long-horizon reinforcement learning tasks and the disconnect between high-level LLM planning and low-level policy optimization.
analysis.executive_summary: This work bridges the gap between high-level semantic planning and low-level motor control by introducing a Progress Reward Model that provides dense, theoretically grounded rewards derived from LLM-decomposed subtasks. It offers a scalable solution for complex robotic manipulation that outperforms both pure planning and pure reward-shaping approaches, enabling more efficient policy convergence without exhaustive human annotation.

key_metrics.baseline: LLM-based planning methods and LLM-based reward generation methods

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses potential-based reward shaping to construct the PRM, ensuring theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees for the RL agent.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not explicitly detailed in the abstract, but implies standard RL training loops augmented with LLM inference for planning and progress evaluation.

paper.title: ClaimScope: Label-Blind Witness Verification for Mathematical Claim Auditing
paper.summary: Mathematical agents are commonly evaluated by answer accuracy or proof acceptance. We introduce ClaimScope, a 72-task benchmark for auditing proposed claims through a verdict, scope, counterexample, and repair. Tasks cover optimizer-state transport, finite-horizon affine recurrences, and exact $2\times2$ linear algebra. We evaluate Qwen3-8B with direct generation and four matched two-pass conditions, each starting from the same draft. A witness checker evaluates only the model's submitted state, without consulting reference verdicts or supplying a replacement witness. Its feedback still conveys information about validity: a verified refutation establishes that the claim is false, and rejection reasons can suggest structural fixes. In this evaluation, verifier feedback yields $23/39$ accepted counterexamples on invalid claims and $25/72$ safe completions, compared with $15/39$ and $20/72$ for checker-free generic feedback. Strict completion remains $17/72$; verdict accuracy changes from $47/72$ to $46/72$. The claim-grouped safe-completion difference is $.094$, with a bootstrap 95\% interval of $[.000,.198]$. All seven task-level gains follow horizon/input-length diagnostics. A post-hoc schema-only correction of the direct outputs reaches the same 25 safe tasks without another model call. These results separate claim classification from executable evidence, while locating the observed gains in witness-structure correction rather than demonstrating broader reasoning improvement.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop (Mathematical Reasoning and AI)

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of rigorous, label-blind verification methods for auditing mathematical claims by distinguishing between correct verdicts and executable evidence (counterexamples/repairs).
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and verifiability of mathematical reasoning in LLMs, specifically the gap between answer accuracy and the provision of valid, executable proof structures or counterexamples.
analysis.executive_summary: ClaimScope introduces a 72-task benchmark that evaluates mathematical agents on their ability to provide verified witnesses (counterexamples or repairs) rather than just correct answers. It demonstrates that verifier feedback focused on witness structure significantly improves the rate of safe completions (valid counterexamples) compared to generic feedback, without necessarily improving overall verdict accuracy.

key_metrics.baseline: Checker-free generic feedback (20/72 or 27.8%)

technical_breakdown.architecture: Two-pass evaluation pipeline: 1) Direct generation of claims/verdicts, 2) Matched two-pass conditions using a witness checker to validate and refine the submitted state.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Tasks involve optimizer-state transport, finite-horizon affine recurrences, and exact 2x2 linear algebra. The checker provides feedback on validity (e.g., verified refutation) and structural fixes, enabling post-hoc schema-only corrections.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Evaluation-based; no training required. Complexity is tied to the execution of the witness checker and the generation of 72 specific mathematical tasks.

paper.title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
paper.summary: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the \emph{Solution Determinacy Property (SDP)}: the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods \textsc{GroupCover} and \textsc{ArrowCloak} are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over $2.4\times$ the full-shielding black-box baseline and recovering near-complete model functionality.To address this vulnerability, we propose \textsc{BiShield-TEE}, a bilateral framework that induces \emph{Ambiguous Solutions} through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that \textsc{BiShield-TEE} confines attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware.Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield-TEE.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

analysis.problem_statement: Unilateral weight obfuscation methods in TEE-shielded on-device LLMs are vulnerable to reverse engineering due to the Solution Determinacy Property, which allows attackers to uniquely determine the obfuscation secret.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Intellectual property protection and security of proprietary model weights during on-device inference.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies a critical structural vulnerability in existing TEE-based LLM protection schemes that renders them insecure against targeted attacks. It proposes BiShield-TEE, a bilateral obfuscation framework that introduces ambiguity in the solution space to prevent key recovery. This work is significant for securing commercial LLMs deployed on edge devices where hardware isolation alone is insufficient against sophisticated reverse engineering.

paper.title: When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark
paper.summary: Muon's gains in data efficiency motivate evaluating its performance under explicit data, time, and tuning budgets. On a single A100 GPU, we compare a reference single-device Muon implementation with AdamW across 17.7M- and 33.6M-parameter causal language models and 2.70M-parameter vision transformers. A common 23-candidate development budget selects configurations evaluated with five matched seeds, full validation trajectories, optimizer-step timing, and a frozen one-shot test. Muon reduces validation-loss area under the curve by 3.25--22.44\% at equal data and lowers test loss in all 20 primary pairs. In this configuration, Muon improves time-normalized loss area} by 19.68--22.31\% on vision, while AdamW is better by 3.38--6.96\% on language. The full Muon optimizer call, including auxiliary AdamW updates, consumes 56.1--69.6\% of training time, compared with 6.1--9.1\% for the AdamW baseline. Muon also has higher expected regret under restricted access to these candidate pools. These results characterize small models with reference kernels; their wall-clock ordering does not establish a ranking for larger models or optimized implementations.

paper.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
paper.summary: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.

It quantifies how the location of a misconception (hypothesis vs. implementation plan) significantly impacts the likelihood of failure, offering insights into the path-dependent nature of agent errors.

paper.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
paper.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

paper.title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
paper.summary: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. Since these artificial triggers are absent in clean datasets, standard knowledge distillation (KD) typically eliminates them, leading to the common belief that KD serves as an effective purification defense. In this paper, we propose DAR (Discover-and-Relabel), a support-persistent backdoor method that retains its behavior even after clean-data distillation. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. Notably, DAR keeps attack success above 96% after clean KD and remains defense-resistant in practice. Project page: https://junhoo.me/backdoor

analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the prevailing assumption that knowledge distillation effectively purges backdoor triggers by introducing DAR, a method that exploits natural data patterns rather than artificial triggers. It demonstrates that backdoors can remain highly effective (above 96% success rate) even after distillation, posing a significant risk to the safe reuse of pre-trained models in production environments.

paper.title: GNN-Guided Local Refinement for Efficient Layout Decomposition with DSA-MP
paper.summary: Multiple patterning lithography (MPL) has been widely used to improve lithography resolution in advanced nodes, but it faces cost limits as feature sizes shrink. Directed self-assembly (DSA) offers a cost-effective complement, extending the resolution of optical lithography to sub-10 nm and beyond. Integrating DSA into MPL (DSA-MP) further enhances the resolution of contact/via patterning. Nevertheless, growing design complexity exposes the limits of existing decomposition methods, which struggle to balance solution quality and runtime, and neglect edge-to-edge spacing constraints of DSA templates, compromising manufacturability. To address these issues, we introduce a new conflict graph model capturing the previously overlooked constraints and develop a local refinement strategy powered by the graph neural network, enabling efficient and scalable layout decomposition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher solution quality with faster convergence than state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robustness across layout scales, design styles, technology nodes, and varying mask counts.

paper.title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
paper.summary: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.

It demonstrates that while inherent inquiry skills are limited, applying educational scaffolding strategies can significantly enhance an agent's ability to perform causal discovery and refine hypotheses.

paper.title: Hierarchical Graph Convolutional Network Approach for Detecting Low-Quality Documents
paper.summary: Consistency within a document is a crucial feature indicative of its quality. Recently, within the vast amount of information produced across various media, there exists a significant number of low-quality documents that either lack internal consistency or contain content utterly unrelated to their headlines. Such low-quality documents induce fatigue in readers and undermine the credibility of the media source that provided them. Consequently, research to automatically detect these low-quality documents based on natural language processing is imperative. In this study, we introduce a hierarchical graph convolutional network (HGCN) that can detect internal inconsistencies within a document and incongruences between the title and body. Moreover, we constructed the Inconsistency Dataset, leveraging published news data and its meta-data, to train our model to detect document inconsistencies. Experimental results demonstrated that the HGCN achieved superior performance with an accuracy of 91.20% on our constructedInconsistency Dataset, outperforming other comparative models. Additionally, on the publicly available incongruent-related dataset, the proposed methodology demonstrated a performance of 92.00%, validating its general applicability. Finally, an ablation study further confirmed the significant impact of meta-data utilization on performance enhancement. We anticipate that our model can be universally applied to detect and filter low-quality documents in the real world.

paper.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
paper.summary: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.

paper.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
paper.summary: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency.   In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MAppPrint achieves 4.9~13.9% improvement in AF precision and 3~6 times improvement in timeliness over state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, MAppPrint is robust in dynamic networking conditions, while achieving a throughput of 10.5 GB/s and a prediction latency of 0.68 seconds.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical security challenge of inferring user activity from encrypted traffic by introducing a graph-based model that captures behavioral correlations rather than just packet statistics. It enables real-time, high-throughput monitoring capable of distinguishing between single and multiple concurrent apps, significantly enhancing privacy protection and network security capabilities.

paper.title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
paper.summary: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors.   Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.

analysis.problem_statement: Approximately counting the occurrences of a given k-node template subgraph in a sensitive undirected graph under the local node differential privacy (LNDP) model.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Privacy-preserving graph analytics in distributed settings where strong privacy guarantees (LNDP) previously limited computable statistics to simple degree distributions, preventing the accurate estimation of complex structural properties like subgraph counts.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper establishes the first optimal noninteractive algorithm for subgraph counting under local node differential privacy, expanding the scope of private network analysis beyond degree distributions. It provides a tight lower bound that demonstrates a polynomial gap between central and local node differential privacy for general graph inputs, resolving a key theoretical separation in privacy-preserving data analysis.

paper.title: LSNR: Learned Sparse News Recommendations with Attentive User Modeling
paper.summary: Current learned sparse approaches for recommender systems, such as STAR, represent a user by concatenating their interaction history into a single query string. For news, this creates two bottlenecks: concatenation collapses a user's distinct reading interests into one flat query, and, because news articles are long-form text, concatenating several news articles quickly overruns the context window of the language model used as backbone and forces quality-degrading truncation.   To address both bottlenecks, we introduce learned sparse news recommendations (LSNR). LSNR encodes each article independently and constructs a sparse user vector by combining learned, attention-based weighting of the per-article sparse representations with a dense-projected expansion at the user level. Experiments on the MIND and EBNeRD datasets show that LSNR significantly outperforms STAR, with these gains holding even in short-history settings where truncation is not a factor. Compared to state-of-the-art dense recommenders, LSNR is competitive in standard settings and it outperforms them when the user history is short. An ablation of the user encoder confirms that learned attention-based aggregation outperforms simpler pooling alternatives. Beyond effectiveness, an additional advantage of LSNR is that it serves from an index an order of magnitude smaller than an uncompressed dense baseline.

analysis.problem_statement: Current learned sparse recommender systems fail to effectively model diverse user interests in news recommendation due to the flattening of interaction histories into single query strings and the context window limitations imposed by long-form article text.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Context window limitations and information loss from concatenating long-form text sequences in large language model backbones.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the scalability and representational fidelity issues in news recommendation by decoupling article encoding from user history aggregation. It enables the use of long-form text without truncation by processing articles independently, which is critical for maintaining recommendation quality in data-sparse or short-history scenarios.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Outperformance of STAR and competitive performance against state-of-the-art dense recommenders, particularly in short-history settings.

technical_breakdown.method: LSNR encodes each news article independently to avoid context overflow, then constructs a sparse user vector by applying learned attention-based weighting to per-article sparse representations and adding a dense-projected expansion at the user level.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Independent article encoder, attention-based user aggregation module, and dense projection layer for user-level expansion.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses attention mechanisms to weight per-article sparse representations, replacing simple concatenation or pooling. Serves from a compressed index significantly smaller than uncompressed dense baselines.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces context length requirements per inference step by processing articles independently, though it requires additional computation for attention-based aggregation and dense projection.
